steps.body: If residuals diagnose a line, they can also steer one. Move the line and every leftover changes; the best line is the one that makes them small AND balanced — some up, some down, summing to about zero, with no pattern. Fit by leftover.
Steer the line by its leftovers.

widget.prompt: Fit the line so the misses are small and balanced: data (1,3), (2,6), (3,7), (4,9).
widget.successFeedback: Around ŷ = 2x + 1 the residuals read 0, +1, 0, 0 — tiny and balanced. No slope or shift improves on that without worsening another point.
widget.slopeFeedback: Watch the ENDS: if the first points sit above your line and the last below (or the reverse), the tilt is wrong before the height is.
widget.offsetFeedback: Slope looks right — now the whole cloud sits off to one side. Slide b until the misses straddle the line.

predict.prompt: When the line is fit as well as possible, its leftovers will be…

options.label: Small and balanced — some +, some −, near-zero total
All slightly positive — lines aim under to be safe

predict.reveal: Four points, one straight line: perfection is impossible unless the data is perfectly linear. The best line SHARES its misses — a +1 here offset by nothing worse elsewhere, no side favored. All-zero residuals on real data would mean the data was invented.

explanationVariants: Under ŷ = 2x + 1: predictions 3, 5, 7, 9 against observations 3, 6, 7, 9 — residuals 0, +1, 0, 0, summing to +1 ≈ 0.
Near-zero residual sum means the line passes through the middle of the cloud, over-predicting about as much as it under-predicts.

widget.prompt: Under ŷ = 2x + 1, the four residuals are 0, +1, 0, 0. What is their sum?

commonErrors.feedback: Add again: 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 1. Near zero, not exactly zero — real fits balance approximately.
Sum the RESIDUALS, not the points: 0 + 1 + 0 + 0.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add the four leftovers, signs included.
widget.successFeedback: +1 total across four points — essentially balanced. A sum far from zero would mean the line sits off-center.

explanationVariants: Lowering b to catch (2,6) exactly drops every other prediction by the same amount, converting three perfect hits into misses.
Improving one residual at the expense of the rest is how you recognize an already-optimal line.

widget.prompt: Shifting the line up by 1 would hit (2, 6) exactly. Worth it?

options.label: No — three zero-residuals become −1s to fix one +1
options.feedback: Total miss grows from 1 to 3. The line was already placed.

options.label: Yes — any exact hit helps
options.feedback: Exactness at one point isn't the goal; small TOTAL miss is.

options.label: Depends which point matters most
options.feedback: Without a reason to privilege (2,6), the balanced line wins.

widget.successFeedback: A good fit is an equilibrium: every adjustment that helps one point hurts others more.

steps.body: This is the idea behind the 'line of best fit' your tools compute: they choose the slope and intercept that make the residuals collectively smallest (squaring them so ups and downs can't cancel). You've been doing by eye what least squares does by algebra.

hints: Must the best line touch any data point at all?
Consider four points at the corners of a tall X pattern — a line through ANY one of them tilts away from the middle.
The best line balances misses; touching a point is neither required nor rewarded.
explanationVariants: The optimal line can pass between every point — what's minimized is total miss, and touching a point buys nothing.
Best fit is a property of the whole cloud, not of any member: the line often threads empty space.

widget.prompt: Can the best-fit line pass through NONE of the data points?

options.label: Yes — it balances misses; touching points is irrelevant
options.feedback: The line minimizes collective leftovers and often threads between all of them.

options.label: No — it must touch at least one
options.feedback: Nothing rewards contact. A line through empty space can leave smaller total misses than any point-touching line.

options.label: It must touch at least two
options.feedback: Two-point lines are how you DRAW a line, not how you FIT one.

widget.successFeedback: Fitting serves the cloud, not the individuals — the best line frequently touches nobody.

explanationVariants: Least squares picks m and b minimizing the sum of squared residuals — squaring stops + and − misses cancelling.
Your eyeball procedure and the formula answer the same question: which line leaves the least leftover?

widget.prompt: Software reports 'least-squares line'. Least WHAT, exactly?

options.label: The sum of squared residuals
options.feedback: Squares punish big misses hardest and stop signs from cancelling — then the sum is driven as low as possible.

options.label: The number of points missed
options.feedback: Every line 'misses' nearly all points; counting them can't rank lines.

options.label: The slope
options.feedback: Nothing minimizes slope — a flat line is not automatically a good line.

widget.successFeedback: You fit by residual all lesson; least squares just makes the judgment arithmetic.

takeaways: The best line makes residuals small AND balanced — near-zero sum, no pattern, no favored side.
Every adjustment trades misses; optimality is when no trade helps.
Least squares formalizes exactly this: minimize the summed squared leftovers.
steps.teaser: Course close: you can now fit a line, use it, and — new — audit it. The residual is the difference between drawing a trend and defending one.
